summary: Centralize creation when callers should not know concrete classes.

body:
Rule. A factory returns instances of a family of types based on parameters or config. Callers depend on an abstraction; creation knowledge lives in one place. Use it when construction is non-trivial or when concrete classes must stay hidden from callers.

Why it matters. Scattered construction freezes dependency direction and duplicates setup logic. Factories help tests inject fakes. Overuse wraps every trivial constructor in ceremony that teaches nothing.

Worked example. NotificationFactory.create(channel) for 3 channels returns EmailNotifier for email, SmsNotifier for sms, PushNotifier for push, each wired with its client. CheckoutService asks the factory and calls notifier.send(order) without importing EmailNotifier. Adding SlackNotifier edits the factory or a registration map once. In tests, inject a factory that always returns FakeNotifier recording calls. Simple widgets with one concrete type and a trivial constructor do not need a factory.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest. [[diagram:create]]

When to use. Use factories when multiple product types share an interface and selection depends on config or user input. Use them at composition roots of apps and services.

When to refuse. Refuse a factory for a single concrete class with a trivial constructor. Refuse factories that are just aliases for construction without hiding anything. Refuse hiding creation so well that debugging cannot find the real type. Refuse abstract-factory ceremony when one parameterized factory method is enough.
